analysis.one_liner: Designates 1.5 million acres of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as protected wilderness.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 42 Senate supporters but never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to a committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add roughly 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska — the coastal plain — to the National Wilderness Preservation System [S2]. Once designated as wilderness under the Wilderness Act, the area would be closed to oil drilling, road building, and motorized vehicle use, permanently [S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who value intact public lands: the coastal plain is calving ground for the Porcupine caribou herd, polar bear denning habitat, and nesting ground for migratory birds that reach every lower-48 state, and a wilderness designation would protect it from drilling and development in perpetuity [S2][S3]. The Gwich'in people, whose subsistence culture depends on the caribou herd, and future generations of the public would also benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, outdoor users, and future generations

how_it_helps.text: Permanently protects about 1.56 million acres of the refuge's coastal plain by adding it to the National Wilderness Preservation System, the strongest legal protection available for federal land [S2][S3].
Under the Wilderness Act, wilderness designation bars oil and gas drilling, new roads, and motorized access, so the protection cannot be undone by a future administration's leasing decisions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, which would be permanently barred from developing what is believed to be one of the last large onshore prospects in the United States. Alaska's state government and some Alaska Native communities would forgo potential revenue and jobs from coastal plain development, since the state relies heavily on petroleum income.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies; Alaska's petroleum economy

drawbacks.text: The coastal plain is the only area of the refuge believed to hold significant recoverable oil, and development would bring federal and state royalties and jobs; supporters of drilling argue that with modern methods a limited footprint could produce energy while leaving most of the plain untouched. Energy development is a core economic engine for Alaska, and drilling revenue supports state services that other states fund with broad taxes.

Some Alaska Native communities on the North Slope, including Kaktovik, sit within the affected area and have supported development as an economic opportunity, so a permanent ban is not universally welcomed even among people who live nearest the refuge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection would be permanent and essentially free to the federal budget, in exchange for giving up uncertain future oil revenue and jobs concentrated in Alaska. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how one values undisturbed habitat and climate goals against domestic energy production; the bill made the trade explicit rather than hidden, but it did not address the economic losses borne by Alaska's petroleum-dependent communities.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate environment committee the same day, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on April 4, 2017, with 39 other senators joining as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction; that was the only action it ever received [S5].
It accumulated 41 cosponsors (40 Democrats and 1 Independent) over the life of the bill, all from outside the Republican majority [S4].
The committee never held a hearing or markup and the Senate never considered it, so the measure expired at the end of the 115th Congress in January 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests, Alaska's political leadership, and others who wanted the coastal plain kept available for drilling were better off, since the land remained legally open to development — and Senate Republicans opened part of it to oil leasing in a tax bill later that same Congress.

for.name: Edward J. Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the wilderness designation bill on April 4, 2017.

for.name: 40 of 47 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: John Barrasso
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee: no hearing or markup in two years.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

against.name: Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan
against.what_they_did: Advocated for opening the Arctic Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas development, opposing a permanent wilderness designation.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 supporters were Democrats and one Independent; with Republicans holding a 51-seat Senate majority, the bill had no Republican cosponsor and never reached the floor.

industries.note: The bill would permanently close the Arctic Refuge coastal plain to drilling, removing one of the largest untapped onshore prospects available to the industry. Development there carries spill and habitat risks the public would bear, so the industry's gain from keeping the area open runs against the conservation outcome the bill sought.

industries.industry: Alaska's petroleum-dependent economy and Native corporations
industries.note: A wilderness ban would cut off potential royalties, jobs, and Native corporate revenue from coastal plain development. Alaska communities are genuinely divided: those near the refuge seeking economic opportunity lose, while Gwich'in villages downstream of the caribou herd gain.
